summary: Defines how Trickle ICE, the incremental delivery of connection candidates, is used with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). Doing so lets SIP calls begin connectivity checks sooner and shortens session setup. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Starting a phone call can feel slow while the phones work out how to reach each other. This document lets the phones share clues bit by bit as they find them, so the call starts faster.

subtitle: How SIP phones can share network address clues in small batches, so calls start before every clue is in.

tldr.problem: Regular ICE makes both sides gather every candidate address, swap them all, and only then start checking connectivity. That blocking sequence delays the start of a SIP call.
tldr.mechanism: Trickle ICE for SIP sends a few candidates (or none) in the first offer and answer, then delivers the rest in SIP INFO requests inside the dialog, using a new Info Package, media type, SDP attribute and option tag.
tldr.outcome: Gathering and checking run in parallel, which shortens session setup. The document is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9725.

facts.label: Pending INFO requests
facts.value: At most one at a time

today: RFC 8840 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9725.

sections.title: Why Trickle ICE Needs a SIP Usage
sections.content:
ICE (RFC 8445) helps two endpoints behind NAT find a working path for media. It has three phases: gather candidate transport addresses (source IP, port and transport protocol), send them to the other side in the SDP body of a SIP message, and check connectivity between all candidate pairs. In plain ICE these phases happen one after another, in a blocking way, and only when they finish can the agents start talking.

The Trickle ICE extension (RFC 8838) lets these phases overlap. This document defines how that works with SIP (RFC 3261): candidates travel incrementally in SIP INFO requests (RFC 6086), and the Half Trickle and Full Trickle modes are chosen depending on what a user agent expects the other side to support.

To do that, the RFC defines a new Info Package, a matching media type, an SDP attribute and a SIP option tag. With plain ICE for SIP (RFC 8839), candidates are exchanged only through SDP offer/answer. Here they can also flow in parallel with an ongoing negotiation, or after it completes.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal ICE is like waiting until everyone has finished packing before the trip starts. Trickle ICE lets the trip begin while people are still bringing bags to the car.

sections.title: The First Offer and Answer
sections.content:
Trickle ICE agents MUST put the SIP option tag trickle-ice in a Supported: header on all INVITE requests and responses, and MUST include the ice-option trickle in all SDP offers and answers. They MAY include any number of candidates, from zero up to the complete set, in the first offer or answer. A complete set in the first offer is called Half Trickle.

If an offerer sends its offer before knowing a candidate for a media description, it MUST set the port to the default value 9. If it does not want to reveal its host address, for privacy reasons for example, it SHOULD use 0.0.0.0 (or :: for IPv6) in the c= line. In that case it cannot know the RTCP address, so it MUST NOT include an rtcp attribute. The answerer follows the same rules for its answer.

Each m= line MUST carry a mid attribute, which later lets trickled candidates be tied to the right media description. A trickled candidate will never match a default address, and that MUST NOT be treated as an ICE mismatch.

Later offers and answers work as in regular ICE (RFC 8839). Candidates already sent in INFO requests SHALL be included in them, and the version number on the o= line is incremented by 1 as RFC 3264 requires. INFO requests themselves are not offers or answers.
sections.plainLanguage: The first message can have a few hints, or none at all. If there are none, it uses a placeholder address that means "I will tell you later".

sections.title: Establishing the Dialog Before Trickling
sections.content:
Trickling can only start when two conditions hold: support for Trickle ICE at the peer is confirmed, and a SIP dialog exists between the peers. An offerer that receives an answer in a reliable provisional response (confirmed with PRACK) satisfies both and can trickle right away.

An answerer that sent its answer in an unreliable provisional response cannot tell whether it arrived. It retransmits the response with the exponential backoff timers of RFC 3262. Retransmission stops when it receives an INFO request carrying a trickle-ice body, any other in-dialog request from the offerer, or when it sends the answer in a 2xx response. For this reason the offerer MUST send a Trickle ICE INFO request as soon as it receives an answer in an unreliable provisional response, repeating the candidates it already sent.

The answerer can also respond with provisional responses that carry no answer at all, just to set up an early dialog, and start trickling. When the final 200 answer repeats an answer already sent in a provisional response, it must be exactly the same, and the offerer MUST ignore the candidate information in that 200 response.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can pass notes, both of you need to know the other person is actually at their desk. A first note back and forth proves it.

sections.title: Candidates in INFO Requests
sections.content:
Each INFO request carries Info-Package: trickle-ice and a body of type application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag. The body is a limited slice of SDP. Because candidate and end-of-candidates lines say nothing about which m= line they belong to, the body uses pseudo m= lines. A pseudo line only marks which real media description follows, via its mid attribute. The receiver ignores the rest of its content. If the sender does not know the real values, it uses defaults: media audio, port 9, proto RTP/AVP and format 0.

Every INFO request MUST carry ice-pwd and ice-ufrag, at the same level as in the offer/answer. A receiver MUST discard an INFO whose values do not match the current ICE negotiation session.

Because requests may be retransmitted or reordered, each INFO MUST repeat all candidates sent before under the same ice-pwd and ice-ufrag, in the same order, with new ones added at the end. The receiver drops candidates it already has (same IP address, port, transport and component ID) and hands the new ones to ICE in order.

An end-of-candidates attribute means the sender will send no more. Before any pseudo m= line it applies to the whole session. After one, it applies to that media description only.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note says which game board its hints are for, and every new note repeats the old hints in the same order, so nothing gets mixed up if one note arrives late.

sections.title: Finding Out Whether the Peer Supports Trickle
sections.content:
A first offer cannot rely on earlier SDP to learn whether the other side supports Trickle ICE. The RFC notes that the SIP discovery tools, user agent capabilities (RFC 3840) plus GRUUs (RFC 5627), have seen low adoption. It offers three options.

  • Provisioning. In controlled deployments the operator may know that endpoints support Trickle ICE, for example when Session Border Controllers connect to user agents that do not. An offerer assuming support MUST include Require: trickle-ice, so a wrong assumption fails visibly and the client can resend without it.
  • OPTIONS and GRUU. A user agent can query capabilities with an OPTIONS request and then address a specific device. This prevents forking for that request.
  • Fall back to Half Trickle. Gather candidates first, send them all in the offer, and trickle only afterwards. It costs extra latency but gives offers that work with both ICE SIP endpoints and legacy endpoints.

Once any offer or answer has been exchanged in a dialog, support is known and later exchanges can use Full Trickle.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send hints early only if your friend understands the game. You can ask first, assume it if you are sure, or play it safe and wait.

sections.title: RTCP Multiplexing and Media Multiplexing
sections.content:
Trickling gives extra freedom when RTP and RTCP share a port. A Half Trickle offerer must include candidates for all components. A Full Trickle offerer can send only RTP candidates (component 1) at first, and gather RTCP candidates (component 2) only if the answer shows that multiplexing is unsupported. An answerer MAY put rtcp-mux in an INFO body, so the offerer can stop gathering or free RTCP candidates before the answer arrives.

The same idea applies to bundling (RFC 8843). A Full Trickle offerer can start with candidates only for the m= line with the suggested bundle address. An answerer SHOULD include group:BUNDLE at session level in its INFO body if it uses bundling. Even after an offerer frees unneeded candidates, it must keep repeating those it already sent in later INFO requests.
sections.plainLanguage: If two friends can share one walkie-talkie channel, there is no need to search for a second channel. A quick note saying so saves effort.

sections.title: Why INFO, and the Rules That Go With It
sections.content:
The RFC picks INFO because it is lightweight. Once a dialog exists, INFO requests can flow both ways with no timing limits and no collisions, and each direction is independent. UPDATE or new offers would not fit: Offer/Answer allows only one active exchange, which would force a candidate pool at each agent, and simultaneous offers cause glare. SIP recovers from glare by retrying after a period between 0 and 4 seconds, which could make Trickle ICE slower than regular ICE. In-dialog INFO also reaches the same entity as the offer, without requiring GRUU support.

Rate rules: an implementation MUST aggregate candidates over an unreliable transport such as UDP, and an agent MUST NOT have more than one INFO request pending at a time. Middleboxes that monitor SIP must stay in the signaling path of INFO requests and understand their bodies.

IANA registrations: the SDP attribute end-of-candidates (media and session level, mux category IDENTICAL), the media type application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag, the Info Package trickle-ice and the SIP option tag trickle-ice.
sections.plainLanguage: Passing small notes on the side is easier than stopping the main conversation each time. The rule is to send one note at a time and not flood the room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6086, RFC 8838 and RFC 8839 apply. The document says it clarifies how those specifications are used together for trickling candidates and does not create additional security risks.

The new Info Package and media type likewise add no new considerations in the context of Trickle ICE. Both are not meant for other applications, so security in other contexts is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This document only explains how to pass the notes. It says it adds no new ways for trouble to happen.
